questions.question: Why can optimizing only pixel-wise MSE lead to blurry generated images?
options: MSE always makes networks unstable
MSE prefers the average of plausible outputs, which can wash out detail
MSE cannot be computed on images
MSE forces the model to use discrete tokens
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts VAE-style reconstruction losses with adversarial training. If several outputs are plausible, MSE rewards their average, and that average often looks fuzzy rather than realistic.

questions.question: In a GAN, what is the discriminator trying to do at a high level?
options: Predict the next token in a sequence
Distinguish real samples from generated ones
Compress images into a latent code
Estimate an exact normalized likelihood
questions.explanation: The discriminator is introduced as a classifier that scores whether a sample looks real or fake. Its evolving judgment becomes the training signal that teaches the generator what currently counts as plausible.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend the non-saturating generator loss -log D(G(z)) instead of log(1 - D(G(z)))?
options: It removes the need to train the discriminator
It gives the generator stronger gradients when the discriminator is confident
It makes GANs compute exact likelihoods
It turns the game into supervised learning
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that the original generator objective saturates when the discriminator confidently rejects fake samples, so gradients nearly vanish. Using -log D(G(z)) flips the behavior and gives the generator a strong corrective signal exactly when D is most certain.

questions.question: What is mode collapse in the lesson's GAN terminology?
options: The discriminator predicts 0.5 for everything
The generator produces only a few outputs or one mode despite diverse real data
The model switches from images to text tokens
Training slows down because batches are too large
questions.explanation: Mode collapse is described as the generator discovering one region of output space that fools the discriminator and repeating it endlessly. The result is poor coverage of the real distribution even if the samples it does produce look sharp.

questions.question: What lasting production advantage do GANs still have according to the lesson?
options: They require the most iterative refinement steps
They always beat diffusion on open-domain quality
They generate in essentially one forward pass with very low latency
They rely on KV-cache optimizations for decoding
questions.explanation: The production note says GAN inference is just a single forward pass through G(z), with no diffusion schedule and no autoregressive decode. That simple one-shot path is why GAN-style distillation remains attractive for very fast generation even after diffusion surpassed standalone GANs in broad quality.
